To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the canonical ensemble is inappropriate for inhomogeneous systems and that the microcanonical ensemble must be used for all systems.
the phase space of a multifragmenting nuclear system is inhomogeneous and that the canonical ensemble is not applicable.
nuclear multifragmentation is not a phase transition of first order but rather a phase separation.

the fundamental principles of phase transitions and phase separations in general, with their relation to the thermodynamic limit, and with their application to nuclear multifragmentation as a microscopic and non-equilibrium system, as a test ground for the fundamental understanding of statistical mechanics.
the fundamental understanding of the physics of nuclear multifragmentation and the relation of nuclear fragmentation to general physics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nuclear multifragmentation is not only a nuclear phenomenon but rather a general phenomenon.
nuclear fragmentation and phase separation are a very interesting and important field for fundamental physics.
nuclear multifragmentation is a very important test ground for statistical mechanics and thermodynamics, in general, and for the basic principles and concepts of statistical physics, in particular.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nuclear fragmentation can be considered as a test ground for the general physics of phase transitions and phase separations, which in turn are the basis for the whole of thermodynamics.
nuclear multifragmentation, the phase transition of first order and the related phase separation, are a unique test ground for statistical physics.
we have found a new, non-equilibrium, statistical description of nuclear multifragmentation, which is in accordance with the experimental data and with basic principles of statistical physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the statistical physics of phase transitions and of phase separation is not only applicable in macroscopic systems, as is well known, but also in microscopic systems.
phase transitions of first order cannot be described by canonical statistics.
the canonical ensemble cannot be used for phase transitions and phase separations in general.
